rag_matches.description: Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

Small to giant trees, with horizontal and whorled lateral branches; sap initially watery and then turning red upon exposure; stipules absent. Leaves simple, alternate, distichous, margin entire, often stellate-pubescent. Flowers unisexual, tiny, actinomorphic; petals absent, tepals generally 3; male flowers: with 2-30 stamens, filaments fused into a column, anthers 2-locular; female flowers: staminodes absent, superior ovary, 1-carpellate, subsessile stigma, 1 ovule, nearly basal. Fruit drupaceous, bivalved, the pericarp somewhat thick, separating longitudinally to expose the single seed covered by a red or white fleshy aril, often conspicuously lacerated. The family consists of 15 genera and around 300 species, pantropical, with 5 genera and 81 species in tropical America; 4 genera (one introduced) and 10 species in Costa Rica; 3 genera and 4 species in La Selva. It is characterized by its whorled and rhythmic branching, long horizontal branches, and simple, alternate, and distichous leaves. These latter characteristics may confuse it with families such as Lauraceae and Annonaceae, but in these, the indumentum consists of simple hairs, while in Myristicaceae it is often stellate, malpighiaceous, or absent (Costa Rica: Compsoneura), as well as by its watery sap from the trunk that turns blood red upon exposure. It is said that the ruminated endosperm of the seeds may indicate that the seeds of this family are among the most primitive of flowering plants. Its unisexual flowers, without petals, small, 3-parted, and generally in open panicles with many flowers. From an economic point of view, the family is well known for nutmeg (Myristica fragans) or plywood wood from species of the genus Virola, Otoba, etc., better known as golden fruit. The aril that surrounds the seeds is an important food source for several species of birds and is a spice in Eastern cuisine.

Functionally unisexual tree, to 18 m tall, to 27 cm dbh; outer bark thin, flaking in firm sheets, lenticellate; inner bark moderately thick, reddish; sap slowly forming viscid, cloudy droplets after slash, with strong, sweet aroma; stems glabrous, prominently brown-lenticellate. Leaves imparipinnate; petioles flattened above with sharp margins; petiolules thickened at both ends; leaflets 5-9 (13), mostly oblong to oblong-elliptic, acuminate with blunt acumen, acute to rounded at base, often ± inequilateral, 10-20(27) cm long, 5-9(12) cm wide, glabrous except for minute papillae. Panicles axillary, near stem apex, the branches ferruginous; staminate inflorescences somewhat larger than pistillate inflorescences (to 24 cm long); flowers 5-parted, sessile, 3.5-5 mm long; calyx to 2 mm long, cupulate, 5-lobed, minutely pubescent, the lobes acute; petals lanceolate, yellow-green, thickened medially on outside, ca 3 mm long, erect to somewhat spreading at anthesis; stamens 10, alternately long and short, the longest to 2 mm long, the shortest to 1.3 mm long, scarcely longer than the prominent, pubescent disk; ovary ovoid, densely pubescent; style short, the ovary and style together ca 2.7 mm long; stigma 5-lobed, persisting in fruit. Capsules drupaceous, bearing 1-5 pyrenes, ovoid to depressed-globose, with 4 or 5 lobes (rarely 2- or 3-lobed), mostly 2-3 cm diam, red at maturity, usually rounded at both ends, the carpels 4 or 5, each dehiscing by a single valve, the valve falling free to expose the white mesocarp surrounding the pyrene; pyrenes black, 1 per carpel, 1-seeded, ovoid in face view, irregular in side view. Croat 11109, 14822. Common along the shore; occasional in the forest. Flowers chiefly in April and May. The fruits mature chiefly in the middle of the rainy season (August to October). Small bees, possibly Trigona species, have been seen visiting the flowers. The fruits are edible. Costa Rica and Panama. In Panama, known only from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Chiriqui Province, Panama, and Darien Province. Reported from tropical wet forest in Costa Rica (Holdridge et al, 1971).

Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Petioles to 2 cm long; blades obovate, rounded at apex (sometimes acute to acuminate on juvenile leaves), acute to obtuse at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, very thick, dark green and glossy above, dull below, coriaceous; veins indistinct, drying with many fine veins. Panicles stout, bracteated, divaricately branched, terminal; buds depressed-globose; pedicels stout, to 1 cm long; flowers thick, 5-parted, spreading at anthesis, to 4.5 cm diam, white to pink, the lobes often marked with maroon or magenta at base or apex; sepals 2, concave, unequal, persisting in fruit; petals 4-10, broadly oblong, 2-2.5 cm long; androecium of staminate flowers cushion-shaped, ca 1 cm wide and 5 mm high with numerous anthers; pollen white, granular, compressed in round or oval pouches ca 1 mm diam, embedded just beneath the sticky surface of the disk; pistillate flowers similar to staminate but the gynoecium divided into (4)9(15) segments, the petals falling soon after anthesis, the sepals closing. Capsules subglobose, 2.5-3 cm long, dehiscing into 5-9 parts at maturity; valves thick, ± spreading to expose the colorful mass of seeds; seeds numerous, reddish, curved-oblong, ca 5 mm long, embedded in a deeply divided, bright-orange aril. Frequent epiphyte in the forest or on exposed shorelines; epiphytic on rocks or on trees near the edge of the water. Plants are usually supported on tree trunks or large branches but the branches may grow into the top of the canopy. Apparently flowers and fruits sporadically throughout the year. Where plants occur along the shore, the branches usually root at the nodes with the roots hanging in the water. The pollen sacs of the staminate flowers burst under the slightest pressure, and abundant pollen oozes out (sometimes explosively). Several species of small bees, including Trigona spp., have been seen visiting the flowers. The geographical range of Symphonia globulifera extends from Nicaragua to Panama, probably to Colombia. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Colon, San Bias, Veraguas, Herrera, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Code (El Valle) and Panama (Cerro Campana), and from tropical wet forest in Code (La Mesa) and Panama.

Life Form: Tree, Shrub 10. Maquira Aubl. By C.C. Berg. Trees or shrubs, dioecious. Leaves alternate, distichous on lateral branches; blade leathery, margins entire, pinnate-veined; stipules not completely amplexicaul, free. Inflorescences on spurs in the axils of the leaves, unisexual, discoid-capitate, involucrate. Staminate inflorescences often several together, pedunculate; flowers not covered by the inner involucral bracts before anthesis, numerous; perianth 4-parted to 4-divided; stamens 4; pistillode absent. Pistillate inflorescences subsessile; flowers numerous; perianth 4-lobed; ovary adnate to the perianth; stigmas 2, tongue-shaped. Fruit-bearing perianth enlarged, fleshy, orange; fruits adnate to the perianth; seed large, without endosperm, cotyledons thick and equal. 4 spp. Tropical America.

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Nearly glabrous liana; outer bark gray, thin, becoming fissured and peeling to expose reddish-brown inner bark; sap sometimes red in older wood. Stipules lacking or minute and early deciduous; petioles short, to 8 mm long; blades ± elliptic, acuminate, rounded or subcordate at base, mostly 6-26(33) cm long, 2-11 cm wide, somewhat coriaceous, the sides ± upturned, broadly undulate. Inflorescences axillary, to 15 cm long, branched many times, fragile; pedicels ca 1.5 mm long, slender; flowers greenish, to 2 mm diam, 5-parted; sepals minute; petals spreading, ca 1 mm long, papillose-puberulent; stamens 3, minute, included. Mericarps 3, divergent, capsular, longer than broad, rounded or emarginate at apex, 7.5-10 cm long, 5-6 cm wide, 1-2 cm thick; exocarp light brown, ± roughened; seeds usually 4 per mericarp, 4-7.5 cm long, 1-1.5 cm wide, fleshy, buoyant, irregularly angulate. Croat 7677. Occasional in the canopy [of the rainforest]; more common at the edge of the lake [in the Canal Zone]. Flowers in the dry season, with the fruits maturing 9-12 months later. Flowering inflorescences disappear quickly. The fruits are quite distinctive and are probably principally water dispersed. Known from Panama and Colombia (Choco). In Panama, known from tropical moist forest on the Atlantic slope of the Canal Zone and in San Bias and Panama (San Jose Island).

Shrub or tree, 1-10(-18) m, the twigs brown; stipules deciduous (but sometimes present with submature leaves). Leaves opposite or with a cuspidate apex, often puberulent and (often) entire or serrated (with the glands of the teeth). Petiole 0.2-0.4 cm, lamina 3.5-11 cm, also hirsute on the midrib on the underside. Flowers with the pedicel articulated at the base; sepals 1/4-1/3 the length of the petals, acute to rounded at the apex, indistinctly 1-3-nerved; petals whitish to pale yellow or orange, 3.5-4.2 mm, glabrous or glabrate; stamens with the connective scale extended laterally and apically (< the total length of the anther), subentire; style 1.252 mm. Fruits 1.5-1.9 cm, slightly velvety; seeds 4-8 mm, glabrous. Wet and very wet forest, 0-600+ m; Caribbean slope and near the Continental Divide, Cordilleras of Guanacaste and Talamanca, Plains of Los Guatusos, Tortuguero, and Santa Clara, Lower Talamanca, Pacific slope N Cord. of Talamanca (Cerro Nara), S Nicoya Peninsula, P.N. Carara, Puriscal region (P.N. La Cangreja), vicinity of Palmar Norte, Gulf Dulce region, Burica Peninsula. Fl. Jan., Mar.—May, Jul., Nov. SE Hond.—Pan. [The fruits with the pedicel articulated at the base and glabrous seeds] easily distinguish Rinorea squamata from its congeners in Costa Rica with opposite leaves. Due to its densely puberulent leaf blades and (often) also hirsute on the midrib on the underside, Rinorea squamata is somewhat similar to Rinorea sylvatica, but vegetatively very different due to its smaller stipules and blades with the glands of the acicular teeth (vs. broadly conical).

Fruits 1.5-1.9 cm, slightly velvety; seeds 4-8 mm, glabrous. Wet and very wet forest, 0-600+ m; Caribbean slope and near the Continental Divide, Cordilleras of Guanacaste and Talamanca, Plains of Los Guatusos, Tortuguero, and Santa Clara, Lower Talamanca, Pacific slope North Cordillera of Talamanca (Cerro Nara), South Nicoya Peninsula, Parque Nacional Carara, Puriscal region (Parque Nacional La Cangreja), vicinity of Palmar Norte, Gulf Dulce region, Burica Peninsula. Fl. Jan., Mar.—May, Jul., Nov. Southeastern Honduras—Panama. Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Monoecious tree, to 27 m tall and 90 cm dbh, with low buttresses; outer bark thick; stems, petioles, stipules, and lower midrib of leaf armed with short sharp spines 1-3 mm long; sap copious, yellowish-brown. Leaves alternate; petioles stout, 1-4 cm long, armed; stipules amplexicaul, 1.5-3 cm long, armed; blades variable, obliquely ovate to oblong-elliptic, obtuse to shortacuminate at apex, obtuse to rounded and inequilateral at base, 10-40(70) cm long, 6-25(35) cm wide, usually glabrous in age, coriaceous. Staminate inflorescences globose, 1-2.3 cm diam, bearing many dense flowers; tepals 4, barely united; stamens 4, slightly exserted. Pistillate inflorescences ovoid, 1-1.5 cm diam, yellowish with (3) 5-9 flowers; perianth 4-dentate; stigmas deeply 2-lobed, exserted. Fruiting heads subglobose or ovoid, to 2.5 cm long, the individual carpels conic, irregularly angulate, sharply pointed at apex, the involucral bracts sharply pointed; seeds 1 per carpel, ovoid, shiny, brown, to 4 mm long. Abundant throughout the [forests of Panama]. Flowers and fruits throughout the year, especially during the dry and early rainy seasons. The leaves, which are somewhat resistant to decay, are usually lost and replaced during the dry season. Red spider monkeys have been seen eating the syncarp. Mexico to Bolivia. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, San Bias, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone, and from tropical wet forest in Colon and Darien.

Tree, to 15 m tall; trunk ca 20 cm dbh; outer bark unfissured, minutely roughened, thin; inner bark reddish-brown, thin, hard; branches enlarged at base; young branchlets and petioles puberulent; sap with faint, pungent odor. Petioles 0.5-1 cm long; stipules minute, paired, subpersistent; blades ovate, acuminate at apex, obtuse to rounded at base, 5.5-10 cm long, 2.5-5 cm wide, glabrous above, whitish below with dense, minute, arachnoid trichomes. Flowers minute, in terminal or upper-axillary panicles 10-20 cm long, the branches and pedicels densely and minutely puberulent; hypanthium campanulate or turbinate, to 2 mm long; calyx lobes 5, minute, ovate, acute; petals lacking; stamens 3, less than 1 mm long; anthers about half as long as filaments; ovary whitehirsute; style to 2 mm long, adjacent to the 2 stamenless calyx lobes. Fruits pyriform to obovate, to 2.5 cm long and 2 cm diam, at first pink to red, becoming white and soft at maturity, usually with a minute depression at apex; mesocarp thick, fleshy, sweet, somewhat pithy; seed obovate, ca 1 cm diam. [Licania hypoleuca] is infrequent, in both the younger and older forests. [Licania hypoleuca] probably flowers in the early dry season. The fruits of [Licania hypoleuca] are mature mostly from April to June. Southern Mexico to Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, and Amazonian Brazil. In Panama, [Licania hypoleuca] is known from tropical moist forest on [Barro Colorado Island] and in [Darien] and from premontane wet forest in [Panama] ([Cerro Azul]).

In Panama, Psychotria brachybotrya is most easily confused with Psychotria involucrata Sw., a superfluous name for Psychotria officinalis (Aubl.) Sw. (Steyermark, 1972). Psychotria brachybotrya differs from Psychotria officinalis by having distinct bracts beneath the lower inflorescence branches and leaves that usually dry a lighter green. Psychotria brachybotrya usually occurs in drier areas than Psychotria officinalis, which occurs principally in premontane wet forest and tropical wet forest.
